governanceNotes: D1 batch 46 (2026-09-24): one bounded association edge authored - hyperhidrosis to anxiety-disorder (rank 1), ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, hypothesizedOnly:true, and mechanismCategory PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL (autonomic emotional sweating and anxiety-related arousal). The proposition rests on the Bahar 2016 study of 2017 consecutive dermatology outpatients, which found anxiety in 21.3% of hyperhidrosis patients versus 7.5% of patients without hyperhidrosis (p<0.001) in a severity-dependent pattern that persisted on multivariable analysis, and on the Kamikava 2021 observational study of 81 patients evaluating anxiety symptoms before and after oxybutynin treatment for primary hyperhidrosis - a severity-gradient anchor plus a treatment-cohort anchor. The edge is not raised to causation: the designs are cross-sectional or observational without incident-anxiety follow-up, the relationship is plausibly bidirectional (anxiety involves sympathetic arousal that itself drives sweating) and shares an autonomic/emotional substrate, and the estimates are of co-occurrence rather than attributable incidence, so no probability estimate is asserted.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Clinical series document a higher prevalence of anxiety in hyperhidrosis patients than in controls: the Bahar 2016 study of 2017 consecutive dermatology outpatients found anxiety in 21.3% of hyperhidrosis patients versus 7.5% without hyperhidrosis (p<0.001) in a severity-dependent pattern that persisted on multivariable analysis, and the Kamikava 2021 observational study evaluated anxiety symptoms in 81 primary-hyperhidrosis patients before and after treatment - a reproducible co-occurrence association rather than an individual causal nexus.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established: the designs are cross-sectional or observational without incident-anxiety follow-up, the relationship is plausibly bidirectional with a shared autonomic and emotional-regulation substrate, and the estimates are of co-occurrence rather than attributable incidence, so an individual determination requires validated anxiety assessment with chronology relative to hyperhidrosis onset and severity, and exclusion of primary anxiety disorder and of medication-, endocrine-, and substance-related sweating.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized psychophysiological route is described: primary hyperhidrosis reflects sympathetic overactivity of eccrine sweat glands and is clinically diagnosed when the excess sweating produces significant emotional and social distress, and the reciprocal limb is that anticipatory anxiety and social vigilance amplify sympathetic outflow to the same glands, so a self-reinforcing cycle of sweating and anxiety can develop - consistent with the severity-dependent anxiety gradient reported in the Bahar 2016 outpatient study and with the anxiety-symptom course followed in the Kamikava 2021 treatment cohort; the cross-sectional design and the shared-substrate confound leave individual attribution hypothesized.
causalMechanism.secondaryVector: Social embarrassment, occupational and relationship limitations, and avoidance behaviour can maintain or worsen anxiety, and the anxiety may in turn increase sweating frequency and severity, which is why the direction is not resolved by the located evidence.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The edge asserts an association only: cross-sectional and observational series show a higher anxiety prevalence in hyperhidrosis patients than in controls with a severity gradient, but the evidence does not resolve direction, the relationship shares an autonomic substrate, and estimates are of co-occurrence rather than attributable incidence; an individual claim therefore requires validated anxiety assessment, documented chronology, and exclusion of primary anxiety disorder and of other sweating causes, so no at-least-as-likely-as-not probability is asserted.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Documentation and characterization of the hyperhidrosis (primary versus secondary, distribution, severity, age of onset, date); validated anxiety assessment (structured diagnostic evaluation or standardized instrument such as GAD-7) with scoring and date; chronology of the anxiety relative to the onset and course of the hyperhidrosis; evaluation for primary anxiety disorder and for medication-, endocrine (thyroid, pheochromocytoma), neurologic, and substance-related sweating; assessment of occupational and social functional impact; dermatologic, psychiatric, or primary-care assessment of whether the hyperhidrosis materially contributed to the individual anxiety
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Primary anxiety or panic disorder independent of sweating
Medication-related (SSRI, opioid, cholinesterase-inhibitor) or substance-related sweating
Endocrine causes of secondary hyperhidrosis (hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, diabetes)
Neurologic or malignant causes of secondary hyperhidrosis

suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: a 2017-outpatient study found anxiety in 21.3% of hyperhidrosis patients versus 7.5% of controls in a severity-dependent pattern that persisted on multivariable analysis, and an observational treatment cohort followed anxiety symptoms in primary hyperhidrosis, establishing a reproducible co-occurrence association; the edge is not raised to causation because the designs are cross-sectional or observational without incident-anxiety follow-up and the relationship is plausibly bidirectional with a shared autonomic substrate, so the consensus remains NOT_ESTABLISHED with validated-assessment, chronology, and competing-cause requirements; no probability estimate is asserted.
